title: The end foretold
where: *Götterdämmerung*, the Prelude and Act 3, with the English of Margaret Armour (1911)
about: *Götterdämmerung* is the last of the four operas of Wagner’s *Ring of the Nibelung*; he wrote the words himself. In the Prelude the three Norns, the Fates, sing as they pass a golden rope, and the third foretells the burning of Valhalla, the hall of the gods. In Act 3 the Rhinemaidens tell Siegfried he will be killed that day unless he gives them the ring; he refuses, and they pass judgment on him. At the end Brünnhilde, at his pyre, sends Wotan’s ravens home and throws the torch.

view.says: Auden told the English Institute in 1940 that the people of the *Ring* behave oddly: their mistakes are ones they know in advance to be mistakes. The audience of *Oedipus Rex* knows what its hero does not; here the actors know as well. His example is Valhalla, set on fire with wood of the World Ash Tree; he asks why Wotan keeps such fuel there.
view.quote: the actors are never tired of explaining exactly what is going to happen and how awful it will be; they deny their own knowledge
view.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 81–82
view.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in the scanned copy at archive.org (item prosetravelbooks0000aude; its catalogue title is that of vol. I, but the text is vol. II), which can be read only through its full-text search, one snippet at a time; the snippets were chained phrase by phrase. The lecture stands at pp. 78-87 (by the editor's note Auden gave it at Columbia University on 14 September 1940, at the English Institute's second annual conference, in the section on literary criticism). Page 81 ends at 'the behavior', where the footnote to Nietzsche's The Case of Wagner stands; page 82 runs from 'of the characters is odd' to 'The final moral would seem to'. Each sentence used was found once only in the volume. NOTE: remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md (section 31 and H17c) gives this passage to 'James Joyce and Richard Wagner', pp. 115-19. That is wrong: that essay (Common Sense, March 1941) is mainly about Joyce and does not contain it.

lenses.label: Stave

threads.sound: of a vowel that opens the word

lenses.caption: These lines do not rhyme. The colored letters are staves, or alliteration: one sound at the head of stressed words, the binding of the oldest German verse. Wagner wrote in 1851 that end-rhyme was a cheat and that this verse bends to the accents of speech. Auden, in 1944, called the words of the Ring alliterative verse full of old and embarrassing expressions; sehrend, wounding, is a word that written German lost early. After the first, the lines pair off: br and h, s and gl, then vowels, which count as alike. Wagner held that a stave makes one image of the words it joins: here ewigen, eternal, and Ende, end.
lenses.why: Wagner gave up end-rhyme for the stave of the oldest German verse because, he wrote, it follows the accents of speech and makes one image of the words it joins; here it joins eternal to end.

grounds.claim: no line ends in rhyme; which sounds come back at the head of which stressed words; after the first line the lines go in three pairs, the first tied by br and h, the second by s and gl, the third by vowels
a stave is the same sound at the head of stressed syllables, and it was the principle of the oldest German and English verse
grounds.source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under Stabreim (vol. X,II,I, col. 377): sameness of the first sound of stressed syllables, above all as the principle of old Germanic verse, whose stressed lifts are called staves. Paull F. Baum, The Principles of English Versification (1922), chapter 5: alliteration, or initial rime, is the agreement of the sounds at the beginning of accented syllables, and the early English, German and Scandinavian prosodies made it a determining principle.

grounds.claim: Wagner, 1851: end-rhyme a cheat; this verse bends to the actual accents of speech; it is the verse the folk once sang
grounds.source: Richard Wagner, A Communication to My Friends (1851), translated by William Ashton Ellis, Richard Wagner's Prose Works, vol. 1 (London, 1892; read in the second edition, 1895), pp. 375-76. He is writing of his Siegfried poem (his note names it Siegfrieds Tod), which Ellis's preface to vol. 8 (1899), pp. vii-viii, describes as the earlier version of Götterdämmerung, scene after scene nearly word for word. Ellis's note at vol. 1, pp. 132-33, says the Ring uses this verse almost throughout.

grounds.claim: Auden, 1944: the text of the Ring is in an alliterative meter and is full of archaic and embarrassing expressions (his word for the second kind is shy-making)
grounds.source: Program notes for a broadcast of Die Walküre (1944), in Prose, vol. II: 1939–1948, edited by Edward Mendelson (2002), Appendix VI, p. 503

grounds.claim: sehrend, one of the three words on the s stave, is from sehren, to wound, a verb the written language lost early
grounds.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under sehren (vol. X,I, col. 164): verwunden, verletzen; the New High German written language lost the word early and keeps it in the compound versehren; it lives on in dialect. The mark on row 4.0, word 0.

grounds.claim: words that open on a vowel count as staves to one another
grounds.source: Wagner, Opera and Drama (1851), part II, chapter vi, in Ellis's translation, Prose Works, vol. 2 (1893; read in the second edition, 1900), p. 227: the likeness of stave-words comes either from a kinship of vowel sounds that stand open in front, with no consonant before them, or from the same first consonant; his own note gives two vowel pairs as examples. Ellis's note, vol. 1, p. 132: where vowels are used they must be of different sound.

grounds.claim: Wagner held that a stave makes one image of the words it joins (the caption then names the two words that the vowel stave joins inside row 5.0)
grounds.source: Wagner, Opera and Drama, in Ellis's translation, Prose Works, vol. 2, p. 227 (kindred roots sound alike to the ear and knit like objects into one collective image). Until 3 October 2026 the caption went on 'opposites too', from p. 291 of the same volume (the Stabreim coupled speech-roots of opposite emotional expression and so presented them to the feeling as akin). The finisher cut those two words: Wagner's examples on that page are of opposite feelings, and that eternal and end are such a pair was the poet's own application (notes.md, section 4). What is left is his general statement and what the marks show: the arc under row 5.0 joins words 1 and 3.

grounds.claim: ewigen means eternal, endless; Ende means end
grounds.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under ewig (vol. III, col. 1200: aeternus; the everlasting, the endless) and Ende (vol. III, col. 447: finis)

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. What a stave is: Grimm’s *Deutsches Wörterbuch*, under *Stabreim*, and Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5. Wagner’s reasons: *A Communication to My Friends* (1851), in W. Ashton Ellis’s translation, pp. 375–76, and *Opera and Drama* (1851), p. 227. Auden on the meter: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 503. *Sehren*, *ewig* and *Ende*: Grimm.

lenses.caption: The opera’s title is never sung in it. Its two halves stand here: Götter, gods, and dämmert. Dämmerung is the half-light of morning or evening, and the title word, on record from 1772, came from confusing two Old Norse names, the fate of the gods and their darkening. With auf, up, the Norn’s verb means to dawn: the end of the eternal gods dawns. Armour keeps the dawn and adds in darkness. The scene’s second line asks, in this verb, whether day is dawning; the answer is that the light is fire. Here too the dawn comes with fire: Valhalla burning with wood of the World Ash, which is Auden’s example.
lenses.why: The Norn foretells the end in the two halves of the title, with a verb that means to dawn; her dawn comes with the fire of the world-ash logs, which is Auden’s example of people who know what is coming.

grounds.claim: the title word is not sung anywhere in the opera
grounds.source: A search of the German libretto (the text of Richard Wagner, Die Musikdramen, Hamburg 1971, as zeno.org gives it; .cache/originals/wagner_goetterdaemmerung_de_zeno.txt): no line of it contains the word Götterdämmerung.

grounds.claim: the two halves of the title stand in the last two lines; Armour keeps Dawn and adds in darkness, for which the German line has no word
Dämmerung is the twilight of morning or of evening
grounds.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under Dämmerung (vol. II): crepusculum; morning and evening twilight

grounds.claim: the title word is found from 1772 and came of a confusion of two Old Norse names
grounds.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under Götterdämmerung (vol. IV,I,V): attested since 1772 among the bardic poets, a false loan-translation of Old Norse ragna rökkr, darkening of the gods, which had been confused with ragna rök, fate of the gods; the word names the downfall of the gods and the world-fire before a new age of the world. The Online Etymology Dictionary, under Gotterdammerung and Ragnarok, gives the same two Norse words.

lenses.label: Against
lenses.name: antithesis
lenses.plain: two opposed things set side by side, often in phrases of the same build
lenses.caption: The Rhinemaidens sum Siegfried up four times, each in two halves: something to his credit, then what stands against it. He thinks himself wise and strong, and is bound and blind. The two middle sentences match, three words then four, both closing on sie nicht, them not: oaths he swore and does not heed, runes he knows and does not read. A highest good was given him, and he does not know he threw it away. Auden says the people of the Ring deny their own knowledge.
lenses.why: Four times the verdict sets something to Siegfried’s credit beside what stands against it; the third says he knows runes and does not read them, and Auden’s charge against the Ring’s people is that they deny their own knowledge.

grounds.claim: four statements of two halves each (the fourth is cut at a semicolon and runs on after the passage); the second and third are sentences built alike, three words then four, both ending on the same two words

what each sentence says: he thinks himself wise and strong and is bound and blind; oaths sworn and not heeded; runes known and not read; a highest good granted, and he does not know he has thrown it away
grounds.source: rows 0.0 to 10.0, with Armour's lines under them. The last sentence does not end with the passage: after a semicolon the German goes on to say that the ring alone, which is to be his death, he means to keep (hosted text, gotterdammerung/act-3, block 97, rows 6-7).

grounds.claim: antithesis is the setting side by side of contrasting words or ideas, often in parallel structure
grounds.source: Gideon O. Burton, Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), under antithesis

grounds.claim: Auden: the people of the Ring deny their own knowledge
grounds.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in Prose, vol. II: 1939–1948, edited by Edward Mendelson (2002), p. 82

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and what its lines say. Antithesis as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. Auden: *Prose*, vol. II, p. 82.

lenses.label: Knowing

notes.note: German *weise* and *weiß*, knows, come from one root, which meant to see: to know was to have seen.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, under wise (adj.), which gives German weise and the root's sense 'to see', hence 'to know', and under wit (v.), which gives German wissen: Proto-Germanic 'to have seen', hence 'to know', from the same root

notes.note: Grimm gives the verb as to suppose or assume, found in written German only in older times, and its simple form *wähnen* as to believe, or to assume falsely.
notes.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under verwähnen (vol. XII,I, col. 2073; sense 2: vermuten, annehmen; sense 3, the same used reflexively; sense 4: to put into a delusion; in the written language only in older times) and wähnen (vol. XIII, col. 650: erwarten, hoffen, vermuten, glauben, falsch annehmen)

notes.note: Grimm: a secret, a secret counsel, a character of the Germanic secret and magic writing; in the Prelude Brünnhilde says she has given him her holy runes.
notes.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under Rune (vol. VIII, col. 1518); hosted text, gotterdammerung/prelude, block 51, rows 8-11
Online Etymology Dictionary, under wit (v.): German wissen

notes.note: The same word as English *read*, whose old senses were to counsel and to interpret; at his death Hagen asks him, in a form of this verb, whether he can make out the ravens’ whisper.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, under read (v.): Old English rædan, to advise, counsel, to read, to explain; German raten, to advise, counsel, interpret, guess; connected to riddle through the notion of interpreting. Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under rathen (vol. VIII, col. 173: adjuvare, consilium dare, divinare). Hagen's question: German libretto, Act 3, Scene 2, the two lines before the spear-thrust (lines 4861-4863 of the zeno text; the verb is erraten and the ravens' sound is Geraun, from raunen, which Grimm derives from the noun Rune); hosted text, gotterdammerung/act-3, block 213.
as above, under wit (v.); Armour's line p:97.5

notes.note: *Rede* is an old spelling of *read* that poets fond of old words kept in use; Wagner’s line has *does not* where Armour has *cannot*.
notes.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, under rede (n.): it has the same source as read; the noun went out of literary use in the 1600s and came back a little in the archaizing and poetic language of the 1800s. The Century Dictionary, quoted there on the verb, calls rede the early spelling of read, used by Spenser and a favorite with the poets who imitated his old words, and says nothing in the word's history supports spelling the two differently. Row 6.0 against p:97.1. Wagner's poem as he printed it in 1872 has the same words in this line (Gesammelte Schriften und Dichtungen, vol. 6, p. 340).

lenses.caption: Words of knowing run through the verdict. Two of them, weise, wise, and weiß, knows, come from one root, which meant to see; the man who thinks himself wise is called blind. Runen are secrets, and letters of a secret script; Brünnhilde gave him hers. The verb rät, the same word as English read, means to counsel, interpret or guess. Wagner’s line says he does not read them; Armour’s cannot is her own. Auden says the people of the Ring explain exactly what is coming and deny their own knowledge. Here the same voices have just told Siegfried he will be killed today, and he keeps the ring.
lenses.why: The verdict is made of words for knowing; its third sentence says he knows runes and does not read them, just after he was told he would die today, and Auden says the Ring’s people deny their own knowledge.

grounds.claim: where the words of knowing stand in the passage; that the one who thinks himself wise is called blind

lenses.label: English

threads.sound: of a vowel that opens the word

lenses.caption: The colored letters are staves, Wagner’s in the German and Armour’s in the English. In his second and third sentences the stave ties what Siegfried has to what he fails to do with it: Eide, oaths, to achtet, heeds, and Runen to rät. In this verse vowels count as alike. Wagner held that a stave makes one image of the words it joins. Armour keeps three of his staves on the same letter: blind and bound, Runes and rede, glorious gift. Two of these are the same words in both languages. The oldest English verse was bound this way too. She drops his w, which opens and closes the passage, and his vowels, and adds an f of her own.
lenses.why: In the two matched sentences Wagner’s stave ties what Siegfried has to what he fails to do with it; Armour keeps three of his staves on the same letter, twice with the same words, and drops two.

grounds.claim: which sounds come back at the head of which stressed syllables, in the German and in the English; that the staves of the second and third sentences fall on the noun of the first half and the verb of the second; that Armour has b, r and g where Wagner has them, no stave on w or on the vowels (her lines under rows 0.0-1.0, 3.0-4.0 and 9.0-10.0), and an f that is not in the German
Wagner held that a stave makes one image of the words it joins
grounds.source: Wagner, Opera and Drama (1851), part II, chapter vi, in William Ashton Ellis's translation, Richard Wagner's Prose Works, vol. 2 (1893; read in the second edition, 1900), p. 227

grounds.claim: in this verse words that open on a vowel count as staves to one another, whatever the vowel (the caption: vowels count as alike), which is why the letters marked in rows 3.0 and 4.0 are a pair
grounds.source: The ground that the Stave tab of the first passage gives: Wagner, Opera and Drama (1851), part II, chapter vi, in Ellis's translation, Prose Works, vol. 2, p. 227 (stave-words are alike either by a kinship of vowel sounds that stand open in front or by the same first consonant), and Ellis's note, vol. 1, p. 132 (where vowels are used they must be of different sound). The finisher, who added the sentence on 3 October 2026, could not open Ellis from where it works, and read instead A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles, vol. I (Oxford, 1888), p. 236, under Alliteration, sense 2: accented syllables of a verse that begin with the same consonant or group of consonants, or with different vowel sounds, as the build of verse in Old English and the Germanic languages generally (the scan ned_oed01arch.txt, lines 99192-99196).

grounds.claim: blind and bound, Runes and rede are the same words as blind and gebunden, Runen and rät
grounds.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, under blind (German blind), bind (Old English bindan, past participle bunden; German binden), bound (the past participle of bind), rune (Old High German runa), read (German raten) and rede (from the source of read)

grounds.claim: alliteration was a ruling principle of the oldest English verse as of the German
grounds.source: Paull F. Baum, The Principles of English Versification (1922), chapter 5: the early English, German and Scandinavian prosodies made it a determining principle

grounds.claim: the stave on w at the head of the passage is in the poem Armour translated as well as in the sung text
grounds.source: Wagner, Gesammelte Schriften und Dichtungen, vol. 6 (Leipzig: E. W. Fritzsch, 1872), p. 340: the poem's first two lines here differ from the sung text, but they too bind weise with wähnt

lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. Wagner on what a stave does, and on vowels: *Opera and Drama* (1851), in W. Ashton Ellis’s translation, p. 227. The words the two languages share: the Online Etymology Dictionary under *blind*, *bind*, *rune*, *read* and *rede*. Alliteration in the oldest English verse: Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 5.

counted in the German libretto (lines 229 and 5395 of the zeno text)

notes.note: The verb that means to dawn, completed by *auf* at the end of the line, as in the first passage.
notes.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under aufdämmern (vol. I, col. 631)

notes.note: The Norn’s line has *ewig da* in this place: forever, then.
notes.source: the first passage, row 6.0, with Armour's line under it, which begins And then. Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under da (vol. II, col. 646): the adverb of place (ibi, there), which often stands in the clause that answers a where; and under the second da, from older dô (vol. II, col. 656), the adverb of time (tum, tunc: at that time, then).

notes.note: The Norn’s words were *den wirft der Gott*, the god throws it.
notes.source: German libretto, the Prelude, the third Norn's second speech (line 303 of the zeno text)

notes.note: The Norn’s word for the fire the god was to throw; Grimm gives it as a burning piece of wood, and English *brand* is the same word.
notes.source: German libretto, the Prelude, the third Norn's second speech (line 299 of the zeno text). Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under Brand (vol. II: titio, torris, the burning piece or log). Online Etymology Dictionary, under brand (n.).

lenses.caption: Brünnhilde’s sentence is the third Norn’s, come true. Götter Ende, the gods’ end, is sung twice in the libretto, there and here, each time with dämmert and auf, dawns. The Norn’s gods were eternal, and their end was to dawn then, da, and forever, ewig. Here the gods are not called eternal, and the word is nun, now. The Norn said the god would throw the fire among the logs; Brünnhilde says werf ich, I throw. She sends Wotan’s ravens home to whisper it, Raunt, Waltraute’s verb in Act 1 for the wish he whispered. Auden observes that she and Siegfried make no new world: they burn with the old one.
lenses.why: The end comes in the words that foretold it, with now where the Norn sang then and forever, and I where she sang the god; Auden notes that the lovers make no new world and burn with the old one.

grounds.claim: the words marked here, set against the first passage: the same phrase and the same verb; the Norn's line has the adjective for eternal and the words for forever and then, this one has neither and has the word for now
the Norn's da, which follows her when-clauses, means then
grounds.source: Grimm, Deutsches Wörterbuch, under da (vol. II, cols. 646 and 656): the adverb that answers a where or a when in the following clause, and the adverb of time (tum, tunc). Armour's line under it in the first passage (p:19.14) begins And then.

lenses.label: English

ties.say: *Rhein* and *Rhine*, like *Raben* and *ravens* two lines earlier, are the same words, so Wagner’s stave on *r* crosses into English.
*Whisper* becomes *tell*. In Act 1 Armour’s Waltraute says *whispered*.
*End*. For this word Armour wrote *downfall* in the Prelude and writes *doom* here.
*Dawns now*. In the Prelude she kept *Dawn*; here the gods are *drawing near*, so in her English the verb does not come back.
*I throw* becomes *thrown be*, with no *I*. In the Prelude her Norn says *is thrown*, with no god.

lenses.caption: Armour stays close, and where the two languages share a word she keeps the stave: ravens and Rhine for Raben and Rhein. Raunt, whisper, becomes Tell. Her English hardly shows that the Norn’s sentence returns. For the same German words she wrote downfall and Dawn in the Prelude and writes doom and drawing near here, so of that sentence only Gods and a stave on d come back. In both places her English names no thrower: is thrown there and thrown be here. Wagner names one each time: the god, then ich, I.
lenses.why: The English keeps Wagner’s stave where it shares his words, but it turns the returning sentence two ways and names no thrower, so the Norn’s prophecy does not come back in Brünnhilde’s mouth as it does in the German.

lenses.caption: The line down the page is the libretto: 2,026 lines of verse in this translation. Each mark is a place where someone speaks of the gods’ end or of Siegfried’s death before it comes: that it will come, or how. The earliest is the third Norn’s, at line 79. Siegfried names the weapon himself, in the oath on Hagen’s spear that Auden, in talk a friend wrote down, called wonderful. The Rhinemaidens tell him the day, and he repeats it to the hunters. Auden says these people never tire of explaining what will happen and how terrible it will be. The spear strikes after line 1,791; the torch is thrown at line 2,002.
lenses.why: Both ends are told again and again, by different voices, before they come, and Siegfried’s by Siegfried himself; Auden’s complaint is that the people of the Ring never tire of explaining what will happen.

auden.says: In the lecture of 1940 Auden tries two readings of the *Ring* as allegory and finds that each goes vague in this opera. To a historian it is the Germany of Wagner’s century: the gods are the old nobility, the dwarfs the men of money, the giants the workers, and Siegfried and Brünnhilde the pair who set the country free; yet at the end the ring only returns to the Rhine. On a psychoanalytic reading one would expect the pair to grow up and marry elsewhere, she Gunther and he Gutrune; the libretto shows those marriages as unfaithfulness that magic has worked, and fatal to both.
auden.quote: Siegfried and Brünnhilde do not create the new world, they go up in flames with the old
auden.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 81–82
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy at archive.org (item prosetravelbooks0000aude), chained phrase by phrase from the top of p. 81 (the running head 'Reviews 1940 81' stands before 'noise, created a taste') to the top of p. 83; the sentence quoted is on p. 81 and was found once in the volume. The psychoanalytic reading stands on p. 82, between the footnote that closes p. 81 and the running head 'Essays and Reviews 1940 83'.

auden.says: Auden took Wagner for the test case of his lecture because he thought him the greatest modern artist and the most typical. The story and its people are allegory, he says, yet Wagner treats them as realistically as opera can, turning recitative, sung speech, into an unending melody that follows the speaking voice. His explanation of the characters’ illogic is the composer: suffering was what Wagner’s art could express, and they act against sense so that he can keep writing the music he did best. For expressing failure, betrayed love like Brünnhilde’s included, Auden ranks him with the greatest geniuses. The best of him, he says, is in the monologues.
auden.source: “Mimesis and Allegory” (1940), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 80–81 and 83
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy at archive.org (item prosetravelbooks0000aude). The sentence on why he chose Wagner ('I choose him because') comes before the list of what the age owes to Wagner, and that list runs over the head of p. 81, so the sentence is on p. 80. The paradox (allegorical plot, realistic treatment, recitative made into melody that keeps to the rhythms of the speaking voice) was chained from 'within the limits of the operatic form' to 'the natural speaking voice', on p. 81. The explanation by Wagner's own suffering, the list of sufferings with Brünnhilde for betrayed love, the judgment that happiness and success were beyond him, and the remark on monologues are on p. 83, which runs from 'be: civilization can only be built' to the footnote citing The Case of Wagner, p. 34, under the running head 'Essays and Reviews 1940 83'. The two words that follow 'recitative' in the entry, 'sung speech', are the critic's gloss of the term, added on 3 October 2026; they are not in the poet's paraphrase of Auden's sentence. The finisher could open no ground for them from where it works: no volume of the dictionary at hand has the letter R. The Orpheus page prints the same gloss on a ground its own finisher opened that day (Treccani, under recitativo: a way of singing that follows the cadences and inflections of speech and makes no closed melody).

auden.says: *New Year Letter*, the long poem Auden published in 1941, says that the hero Wagner put on the stage has done all his thinking once he knows that his ruin is fated, and lives to suffer. The note to those lines makes the same charge as the lecture. No Romantic artist is greater than Wagner, it says, because none goes further in the Romantic heresy of setting the necessity of cause above the necessity of logic. The operas are masterly case histories of people in trouble and, as plots, absurd: the fire at Valhalla, fed with wood of the World Ash, is the instance here too.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (1941), lines 1432 ff., p. 66, and the note to line 1432, pp. 143–44
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy of the Faber edition at archive.org (item newyearletter0000aude), chained phrase by phrase. In this edition the page numbers stand at the foot of the page: the last line of the Letter is followed by 75 and then the heading of the Notes; the pages before The Quest and the Epilogue end with 160 and 182, and the contents page gives The Quest 161 and Epilogue 183. The number 143 falls inside the sentence about mistakes, so the note begins on p. 143 (the greatest Romantic artist, the heresy, case histories and absurd plots) and goes on to p. 144 (knowing beforehand, Oedipus, the fire, Mozart). The number 65 falls one line before line 1432 (the examiner searched the scan again: it stands before the line that ends the sentence before), so the verse stands at the top of p. 66. The note also says that for spontaneous happiness, friendship and requited love one must go elsewhere, to Mozart; the piece leaves that out. remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, section 31, gives two of the verse lines from the Collected Poetry of 1945.

auden.says: In 1944 Auden wrote notes for a college radio broadcast of *Die Walküre*, the second opera of the cycle. He says there that Wagner’s text for the *Ring*, dated by him to 1853, is in an alliterative meter full of old and embarrassing expressions.
auden.source: Program notes for a broadcast of *Die Walküre* (1944), in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 503
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy at archive.org (item prosetravelbooks0000aude), chained from the editor's headnote through the opening paragraphs. The headnote dates the notes to the spring of 1944 at Swarthmore: an undergraduate, H. C. Robbins Landon, was in charge of music at the college's radio station and got teachers to write notes for its evening concerts; he read Auden's out himself, before the broadcast and between the acts; the printed text follows the manuscript in the Berg Collection. Page: the running head 'Auden on the Air 503' stands a few lines before the title; the head '504 Appendix VI' follows the opening paragraphs; the volume's index gives 'Walküre, Die, 503'. The sentence on the meter and the list of beings are in the opening paragraphs, on p. 503. The sentence on what the later operas hold is in the summary of Act 3, after the running head 'Auden on the Air 505', which falls near the end of the summary of Act 2; the notes end before Appendix VII. He also offers there a reading of the myth as psychology (he takes Valhalla for consciousness, and the river and the caves for what lies beneath it), which the piece does not use. Not in remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md. The finisher (3 October 2026) cut two sentences from the entry: that he lists the Norns among the beings of the Ring (p. 503), and what he tells his listeners the later operas hold for Siegfried (p. 505). They only showed that he named things, and no caption leaned on them; they are kept whole at the end of notes.md. What remains is the sentence on the meter, which this record and the examiner's (exam.md, section 5) put on p. 503, so the page reference was narrowed to that page. The volume is not among the scans on this machine, and the finisher did not open it again.

auden.says: Alan Ansen, a friend who wrote down Auden’s conversation between 1946 and 1948, has him say that just three Wagner operas please him from beginning to end: *Die Walküre*, *Götterdämmerung* and *Tristan*. Within the *Ring* he puts this one second, after *Die Walküre*, and he names two things in it: the oath on the spear in Act 2, which he calls wonderful, and the duet of Brünnhilde and Waltraute in Act 1.
auden.source: Alan Ansen, *The Table Talk of W. H. Auden*, edited by Nicholas Jenkins (1991), p. 16
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy at archive.org (item tabletalkofwhaud0000anse). He gives his order within the Ring (Die Walküre, then this opera) and goes straight on to the oath and the duet; the remark on the duet is followed at once by the running head 'W. H. Auden 17', so all of it stands at the foot of p. 16. Ansen's record runs from November 1946 to April 1948. On p. 44 of the same book (the head of p. 45 follows about 150 words later) Auden says Wagner meant little to him before he read Nietzsche's The Case of Wagner, and the editor's note says he read it soon after he arrived in the United States in 1939; the piece gives that from his own text in The Dyer's Hand.

auden.says: In a BBC talk of 1955 on Tolkien, Auden sets Wagner’s ring beside Tolkien’s. The allegory of the *Ring*, he says first, is only political and psychological: Wotan is no true god, just an old feudal lord, no wiser and no better behaved than anyone else. Each ring gives its wearer rule over the world, and each can be made only by someone who gives up love. Wagner’s ring, because of Alberich’s curse, brings bad luck on every owner, yet it leaves them uncorrupted. Siegfried himself, although the woodbird has told him what it is, takes no interest in it and comes close to handing it back to the Rhinemaidens.
auden.source: “History, Feigned and Real” (BBC talk, 1955), in *Prose*, vol. III (2008), pp. 689–90
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy at archive.org (item trent_0116405823828; its title page reads Prose, Volume III: 1949-1955, Princeton University Press, copyright 2008), chained phrase by phrase. The editor's note says Auden recorded the talk, on Tolkien's The Return of the King, that it was broadcast in the BBC Third Programme on 16 November 1955, and that the printed text follows a transcript kept at the BBC Written Archives Centre; the index gives the talk at p. 686. The running head 'Auden on the Air 689' stands before the comparison with Wagner; the head '690 Appendix V' stands between the sentence on Sauron's mistakes and the sentence on Alberich's curse, so the sentences on the curse and on Siegfried are on p. 690 and the sentences on Wotan and on the two rings on p. 689. Not in remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md. The place in the opera that his last sentence describes is Act 3, Scene 1: before the warning Siegfried takes the ring from his finger and holds it up for the Rhinemaidens, and they tell him to keep it until he has felt the harm in it (hosted text, gotterdammerung/act-3, blocks 71-79; read again by the finisher on 3 October 2026). Until that day the caption of the Against tab reported this remark, with two grounds of its own; the finisher cut it there, because nothing in the figure drawn on that tab is about the ring.

auden.says: Nietzsche’s *The Case of Wagner* was on the list of critical reading Auden recommended for the Michigan course, and the lecture of 1940 quotes it twice. In *The Dyer’s Hand* he says Nietzsche’s book first opened his ears to Wagner, and rates it above any other critical study of one figure he knows: an attack that never lets the reader forget how great its subject is. Elsewhere in *The Dyer’s Hand* Auden is mostly against opera sung in translation, because a listener hears syllables and not words. Wagner in English is unbearable to hear, he says, however good the translation: the new syllables do not fit the notes.
auden.source: *The Dyer’s Hand* (1962), pp. 48 and 473; Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), p. 27
auden.checked: Read on 2026-10-03 in the scan of The Dyer's Hand (research/auden/dh.txt): lines 2527-2534, in 'Making, Knowing and Judging', between the running heads of p. 48 (line 2507) and p. 49 (line 2553); and lines 22276-22288, in 'Notes on Music and Opera', between the running heads of p. 473 (line 22253) and p. 474 (line 22301). On p. 48 he also calls his earlier notions of Wagner silly; the piece leaves that out. The two footnotes to The Case of Wagner in the lecture of 1940 are at Prose, vol. II, pp. 81 and 83, each under a passage quoted from it. The course's list: read on 2026-10-03 in snippets of the scanned copy of Miller's memoir at archive.org (item audenamericanfri00mill). After his sentence on the required books and the opera libretti, Miller, who was in the class, writes that a list of recommended reading went with them and gives eighteen titles; Nietzsche's stands between Eliot's Selected Essays and Thomas Mann's Past Masters. Just before, he has Auden tell the class that he recommends other books as well as the required ones. The page: the book's index gives 'Tristan and Isolde, 27, 75', and the sentence on the libretti, which names that opera, stands immediately before the list. remake/research/A_michigan_course.md, section 1.5, gives the same list from p. 27 (verified there in the scan) and the heading of the mimeographed sheet, Recommended Critical Reading.

auden.says: Reviewing a life of Wagner in 1969, Auden sets out the theory of Wagner’s *Opera and Drama* (1851): the words matter as much as the music, or more; nobody sings together with anybody else; no word is said twice; regular meter is to be left alone, and rhyme too. Only *Das Rheingold* and Acts 1 and 2 of *Die Walküre*, he says, keep its rules. *Götterdämmerung* has, in a phrase he quotes, poisoned drinks, an ensemble of plotters and a massed chorus, and Bernard Shaw, he says, was right that it shares a good deal with Verdi’s *Un ballo in maschera*.
auden.source: “The Greatest of the Monsters,” in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 251–52
auden.checked: Read by the finisher on 3 October 2026 in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords (research/auden/fa.txt), when this entry was put back in the list in place of the close of the same review (the Dutchman page reports that close; it is whole at the end of notes.md). The theory, in five numbered points, is at lines 12035-12059, p. 251; the entry gives the first two (the words; no duets or ensembles, no repeated words, no strict meter or rhyme). The works that conform, and Shaw's remark, are at lines 12066-12095, p. 252. Auden says there that the theory is at bottom an attack on opera made for singers, that Wagner stayed true to that, and that only those two works conform to what he calls its positive dogmas; the entry's 'its rules' are those. The list of what Götterdämmerung has stands in quotation marks inside Auden's sentence, after a passage quoted from Gutman; whose words they are was not traced, so the entry says 'in a phrase he quotes'. The phrase has a fourth item, stage surprises in the manner of Scribe, which the entry leaves out. The remark on Un ballo in maschera is Shaw's as Auden reports it, and 'quite rightly' is Auden's; where Shaw made it was not looked up. Auden does not name Verdi in that sentence: the next essay in the book, on Verdi's letters, names the opera among his (line 12312). Pages: the contents page (lines 114-115) gives this essay at 244 and the next at 256; the foot numbers 244, 247 and 248 stand at lines 11715, 11867 and 11917; seven running heads follow, the title and the author's name by turns, at lines 11921, 11967, 12012, 12063, 12110, 12158 and 12209, which are pp. 249 to 255. The date and the book reviewed are in the book's list of first printings (lines 25005-25007): The New Yorker, 4 January 1969, a review of Robert Gutman's Richard Wagner: The Man, His Mind, and His Music. Tested with build/tools/runs.py against the scan: the entry shares no run of five words with it (two runs of four, one of them the title of Verdi's opera). As the poet first wrote it, the entry gave the quoted list as Auden's own reasons and shared a run of five words with his sentence on rhyme; both were mended. Kept out of the piece: on p. 249 (lines 11940-11945) he says Wagner should be taken fast and recalls a very slow performance of this opera under Knappertsbusch; at the head of p. 253 (lines 12113-12114) a quoted passage speaks of a love theme from Die Walküre that goes with Brünnhilde's devotion to her horse.

Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), p. 27: the list of recommended reading for the Michigan course, by a student who took it. Not seen in full.

Richard Wagner, *A Communication to My Friends* and *Opera and Drama* (both 1851), in *Richard Wagner’s Prose Works*, translated by William Ashton Ellis: vol. 1 (second edition, 1895), pp. 132–33 and 375–76; vol. 2 (second edition, 1900), p. 227.

Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, *Deutsches Wörterbuch*, in the online edition at dwds.de: Götterdämmerung, Dämmerung, aufdämmern, ewig, Ende, da, sehren, Stabreim, Rune, raten, raunen, wähnen, verwähnen and Brand.
Online Etymology Dictionary: wise, wit, read, rede, rune, blind, bind, bound, brand, raven, Rhine, Gotterdammerung and Ragnarok.
Paull F. Baum, *The Principles of English Versification* (1922), chapter 5, on alliteration.
caveats: The German printed here is the text as sung. The poem Wagner printed in 1872, which Armour’s English appears to follow, words the first three lines of the second passage a little differently, with *strong* before *wise*, and has another word for *once* in the first.

Auden’s lecture of 1940, his radio notes of 1944, his talk of 1955, the verse and note of *New Year Letter*, Ansen’s *Table Talk* and Miller’s memoir were read only in snippets of scanned copies, a sentence at a time, and not in a full copy.
The praise of the oath on the spear comes from a friend’s record of Auden’s talk, not from Auden’s own text.
Which lines count as telling an end beforehand is a judgment. The drawing marks places where a character says that the end will come, or how; other lines only hint at it or call for it.
A stave is a matter of the ear. In the first line of the first passage *Weltesche* can be heard to bind with *war*, and that is left unmarked.
open: The research notes are wrong about where Auden's main passage on the Ring stands. remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md (section 31, H17c) gives the sentences on Siegfried and Brünnhilde going up in flames, on characters who know beforehand, and on Luther and Hitler to 'James Joyce and Richard Wagner' (Common Sense, March 1941; Prose II, pp. 115-19). They are in 'Mimesis and Allegory', the English Institute lecture of 14 September 1940 (Prose II, pp. 78-87; the Ring at pp. 81-83). So the date is 1940, not 1941. Any other piece that cites this passage from the notes (Tristan, the Dutchman, Joyce) should be checked. The notes also lack three things used here: Auden's program notes for a broadcast of Die Walküre (Swarthmore, spring 1944; Prose II, Appendix VI, pp. 503-5), where he describes the verse of the Ring as alliterative and as full of old words and of words that embarrass (his own word for those is shy-making); his BBC talk on Tolkien, 'History, Feigned and Real' (16 November 1955; Prose III, Appendix V, pp. 689-90), which compares Wagner's ring with Tolkien's and speaks of Siegfried and the Rhinemaidens; and The Dyer's Hand, p. 473 (he is against opera in translation, and cannot bear Wagner in English). The Dyer's Hand, p. 48, on The Case of Wagner, is in the notes, but under the critical list of part four and not under this work; so is his sentence in Forewords and Afterwords, p. 253, that Nietzsche is the best guide to Wagner. The notes do not have the close of that review (p. 255), on what Wagner's heroes are. It was in this page's list until 3 October 2026, when the finisher took it out because the Dutchman page reports the same paragraph (the entry is whole at the end of notes.md); the list here now gives pp. 251-52 of the review, the theory of Opera and Drama and Shaw's remark on this opera. The other Wagner pieces may want all of these.

Auden's lecture of 1940, his radio notes of 1944, his talk of 1955, the verse and note of New Year Letter and the Table Talk could be read only through archive.org's full-text search, snippet by snippet (The Dyer's Hand and Forewords and Afterwords were read in the scans on this machine). The page numbers rest on running heads, footnotes and the index seen in the snippets: Prose II p. 80 (inferred: the sentence stands before a list that runs over the head of p. 81), pp. 81, 82, 83, and pp. 503 and 505 (the head of p. 503 stands just before the title, the head of p. 504 after the opening paragraphs, the head of p. 505 near the end of the summary of Act 2, and the index gives Die Walküre at 503); Prose III pp. 689-90 (heads of both pages seen); New Year Letter p. 66 and pp. 143-44 (the numbers 65 and 143 fall inside the passages; that they stand at the foot of the page was settled from the ends of the Letter, the Notes and The Quest); Table Talk p. 16 (the next words carry the head of p. 17) and p. 44 (the head of p. 45 follows about 150 words later); Miller's memoir p. 27, also read only in snippets (its index gives Tristan and Isolde at 27 and 75, and the sentence that names that opera stands immediately before the list of recommended reading; the research notes give the same page from the scan). The archive.org item for Prose II carries the catalogue title of vol. I.

The German on the plates is the sung text (zeno.org, from Die Musikdramen, 1971). Wagner's poem of 1872 (Gesammelte Schriften und Dichtungen, vol. 6) reads differently in the first three lines of the second passage (strong before wise; the plain verb wähnt; no doch) and has sonst for einst in the first line of the first passage. The sung reading was confirmed only in OCR of vocal scores and later librettos found through archive.org search, not in a score seen page by page. That Armour translated the poem and not the sung text is an inference from her wording: dauntless and wise, in the poem's order; no word for the hero; and in the third passage a dash after Thus, where the poem has a dash after so (vol. 6, p. 361) and the sung text has none.

The third lens of the third plate is a shape. The artist has since given it a drawing of its own (site/js/pieces/gotterdammerung.js; art.md, section 1). Its facts are: lines, parts[] (name, lines, read), ends[] (name, told[] of line, who, says, read; comes of line, who, what, read) and passages[] (name, first, last, read). The script reads all of them when the page runs, so a changed says or name shows in the drawing by itself.

The poet did not see the page drawn (a poet may not build or photograph it) and tested this reading with the checker and by reading the kit's code. The page has since been built and photographed by the examiner, the artist, the critic and the finisher. The poet left three things to look at; what was found is at the end of this note. (1) All three plates are set line under line (as many English rows as German). In the kit as it stood at 07:45 UTC on 3 October (lens-figure.js, lens-rhyme.js and plate.js were read again then), a stroke of a figure and a dotted thread of sound go from one line to the next only where the two rows are neighbours in the plate's list of rows and no line of type lies between them, and in a line-under-line plate the English row stands between two German rows. If that is so, the staves that bind two short lines (most of them here: the Stave tab of the first passage, the English tab of the second) will show by the color of their letters and by points under them, with no join, and the three strokes the Against tab asks for (its join: the two halves of the second, third and fourth sentences) will not be drawn; the kit's own rule is that such parts are told by their color. (2) The English tab of the second passage has six threads of sound, each in a color of its own; if six are too many to hold, the f thread, which is Armour's own, is the one to drop, with the last clause of the caption. (3) Row 9 of Armour's lines in the third passage opens with two words joined by a dash; the tie on it names the second of them. What was found: (1) is so. No stroke joins one German line to the next while an English line lies between them, and the two halves and the staves are told by color (art.md, section 3, fault 2); whether the plates norn and rhine should set the English beside the German is proposed by the artist (art.md, section 4) and is the lead's to decide. (2) The six colors hold; the fourth, a slate, looks faint on its letters (art.md, section 3, fault 6). (3) The tie stands on the second of the two words (the pictures of that tab).
The record on hand for this opera is the funeral march, which has no words, so no passage here is tied to it.

From the examiner (3 October 2026; the full record is exam.md). Every mark, count, dictionary entry and page was opened again, and the page was built and looked at. What was changed in the reading: (1) the Against tab no longer says the verdict 'is close to' what Auden says; it reports his two remarks as he made them, the one of 1955 with its own point, that the ring does not corrupt Siegfried, and its grounds now name the place in this scene where he offers the ring (the finisher has since cut the remark of 1955 from that caption, with those two grounds, because nothing in the figure drawn there is about the ring; the remark stays in the list under the passages); (2) Knowing: the root of weise and weiß meant to see (to have seen is the Germanic verb made from it), rät is glossed from the two dictionaries as counsel, interpret, guess, and the reflexive verb of the second line is glossed fancies himself, with Grimm's remark that written German has it only in older times; (3) Dawn and Now: the verb with auf 'means to dawn' and is no longer called the verb for daybreak (most of Grimm's examples are of hopes and times to come); (4) Now: in Act 1 the whisper verb is not Wotan's alone; Brünnhilde uses it herself when she sends Waltraute back with her refusal (German line 1995), and the caption, the note and the grounds now say whose verb it is; (5) the English tab of the second passage says that Armour lets go the vowel stave as well as the w; (6) the reasons given for Against, Knowing and Told set Auden's sentence beside what the lines say and no longer call the lines his complaint; (7) in the list under the passages the talk of 1955 follows Auden's own order and says 'takes no interest', which is his, where it had 'cares nothing'; the one word quoted from the notes of 1944 is no longer printed; (8) the page of New Year Letter: the number 65 falls one line, not two, before line 1432 (the page is still 66). What the examiner could not do: see Auden's lecture, notes, talk, poem and Ansen's and Miller's books other than in search snippets; check the sung German against a score. What others should look at: the Told tab was still the kit's table when this was written, and the artist has since drawn it; on the English tab of the second passage the dotted strokes of the r and g threads run from Wagner's word to Armour's word beneath it and on to the next line, so the two languages zigzag together, and an artist may want to keep each language's strokes apart; on the Against tab no stroke is drawn between the halves (an English line lies between them), and the halves are told by their two colors, which reads clearly.

From the finisher (3 October 2026; the full record is the last section of notes.md, and the reading as the critic left it is finisher/before.json). Changed: the list gives pp. 251-52 of the review of 1969 again and no longer its close; the entry on the radio notes of 1944 lost two sentences and its page is now p. 503; the Against caption no longer reports the remark of 1955; the Stave caption no longer says 'opposites too'; the English caption of the second passage says that vowels count as alike; two strings in the facts of the Told drawing were reworded. Still open: the finisher could not open Prose II and III, New Year Letter or Ellis's Wagner, so the page narrowed for the notes of 1944 and the first ground for the vowels rest on the poet's and the examiner's reading (the rule for vowels was checked in A New English Dictionary, under Alliteration); the Tristan page gives three of the rules of 1851 from the same two pages of the review; whether the first two plates set the English beside the German is the lead's, and every sentence holds either way.
